note: Golden vectors for the Finance Engine. The server test runs these against functions/finance/engine.js; every platform's mirror must run the same file and produce the same numbers. Adding a case here is how a rule becomes real. Spec: docs/finance-engine.md.

cases.name: decision example: standard VAT is extracted from the price the customer pays
cases.why: NivaDesk_Urun_Kararlari_20260903.md §2 — £120 at 20% is £20 of VAT, not £24.

cases.name: decision example: the margin scheme deducts the purchase price and nothing else
cases.why: Purchase 1500, sale 2000, margin 500, VAT 500 x 1/6 = 83.33. The old Profit type also deducted the fee, the shipping and every expense, which declared less VAT than the scheme allows.

cases.name: decision example: gross margin is revenue less direct cost
cases.why: Revenue 2000, product cost 1200, gross margin 800. Fees and shipping are not part of it.

cases.name: the composite order the survey used against all five old implementations
cases.why: Paid 1500 + remaining 500 + a listed receivable 200 + an orphan receivable 100; purchase 1200; fee 3%; shipping 20; expenses 150 and -50; margin scheme at 20%. Every old layer produced a different number for this order.

cases.name: hiding the base cost in the card settings does not change a single figure
cases.why: The product decision is explicit: UI visibility is separate from accounting. The web and Swift both removed the base cost from profit when it was hidden.

cases.name: a refund reduces the profit
cases.why: The decision lists refunds as a deduction. The fixture matters as much as the rule: every writer of refundedAmount — the bank link, and the Woo, Shopify, Etsy and envelope mappers — ALSO lowers paidAmount by the same money, and the field is read-only on every screen. So the shape below is what production writes, and the £1,000 the sale was worth has to be reconstructed before the refund is taken off it once.

cases.name: a negative expense is a credit and raises the profit
cases.why: The server turned every amount at or below zero into zero; the clients kept the sign. Clamping silently changed money.

cases.name: an amount with no heading still counts, and is reported
cases.why: Swift and one of the two web rules dropped it, so a total came out smaller than the rows it was built from.

cases.name: no VAT method owes nothing
a workspace that is not VAT registered owes nothing whatever the rate says
prices quoted without VAT add it on top
cases.why: Every workspace today is inclusive, which is why the default stays inclusive. This is the new setting.

cases.name: invoice lines decide what the order is worth
cases.why: The line-items-only rule the invoice renderers already follow.

cases.name: selling at a loss under the margin scheme owes no VAT
the order's own method overrides the workspace default
before the tax milestone the margin scheme applies
cases.why: financialTaxTypeForPaymentDate has always switched method on this date; the engine keeps it.

cases.name: on and after the tax milestone the standard scheme applies
an amount stored in another platform's format is read as the person meant it
cases.why: Values reached customFields from text fields on four platforms over two years.

cases.name: the platform fee follows the revenue, including the custom receivables
an empty order is all zeros rather than NaN
a shop that told us what it charged is believed over the workspace's percentage
cases.why: The percentage is a stand-in for a number only the platform knows. Where a connector has the real figure, using the estimate instead is a second, disagreeing definition of the same cost.

cases.name: a paymentFee with no platformFeeKnown beside it is the old estimate, and is ignored
cases.why: Every existing writer puts the percentage estimate into paymentFee, so the presence of a number proves nothing. Without the flag the engine must go on computing its own, or an order edited on any screen would take its estimate as gospel.

cases.name: a shop that really charged nothing is not quietly given the percentage
cases.why: This is the whole reason the flag exists: without it there is no way to tell a real fee of zero from a field nobody has filled in.

cases.name: a fee stored as a negative is still a cost
cases.why: Etsy and PayPal report fees as money out. Subtracting a negative would add it to the profit.

cases.name: a shop's own tax is the VAT due, not a rate the shop never sent
cases.why: Every channel mapper writes taxRate 0 because no shop API returns a rate. The engine used to gate VAT on the rate, so a real £120 of tax on a £1,000 sale reported as no VAT at all.

cases.name: tax a marketplace collects and remits is not the studio's VAT
cases.why: Etsy collects and remits in some jurisdictions. Counting it as the studio's output VAT overstates a return that cannot be recovered from the number alone.

cases.name: a tax nobody has claimed is shown, left out of VAT, and flagged
cases.why: Guessing wrong overstates a VAT return in one direction and understates it in the other. The engine refuses both and asks.

cases.name: a shop that charged no tax is believed, and the workspace rate does not fill in
cases.why: taxAmountKnown is what tells a real zero apart from a field nobody filled in — the same distinction platformFeeKnown makes for the commission.

cases.name: without the flag nothing changes: the rate still rules
cases.why: A manual order carries NivaDesk's own taxAmount, computed from the rate. Reading it as a shop's figure would replace the engine with a stale copy of itself.

cases.name: tax added on top of the price raises what the customer pays
cases.why: A shop knows per order whether tax sits inside the price or is added to it; the workspace setting is only the fallback.

cases.name: a shop's tax figure does not reach a workspace that is not VAT registered
cases.why: Registration is the workspace's own fact and outranks anything a shop says.

cases.name: a refund on an order that carries lines is unchanged
cases.why: An order with lines is worth what its lines say, so the refund was never inside the revenue and is subtracted once as before.

cases.name: the margin scheme ignores a shop's tax figure
cases.why: The margin scheme's VAT is computed from the buying and selling price, which no shop knows. Using its figure would apply the wrong scheme's answer.

cases.name: a known fee is rounded once, on every platform
cases.why: Two mirrors rounded a known fee and two did not, and netProfit subtracts it — so the four implementations sat a penny apart on a fee with three decimals. The engine rounds it where it is computed.

cases.name: an empty vatMethod falls through to the setting the workspace has always stored
cases.why: The server's || treats an empty string as absent; Swift's ?? and Kotlin's ?: fire on null only, so a workspace with vatMethod "" beside taxCalculationType Profit took the standard scheme on two platforms and the margin scheme on the others.

cases.name: a placeholder rate of zero does not zero the margin scheme
cases.why: Channel mappers write taxRate 0 because no shop API returns a rate. With the amount known that zero holds no information, so the workspace's own rate has to stand for the one calculation a shop cannot do.

cases.name: money stored as text is read, not treated as nothing
cases.why: Order fields have been text on this platform for years. A runner that reads only JSON numbers reports zero and stays green while the mirror is right — so the vector carries strings on purpose.
